topic: How Fidel Castro nationalized Bacardi's Cuban distillery in 1960, but failed to take the secret yeast strain that made Bacardi rum unique.

script: Fidel Castro seized the Bacardi distillery in 1960 and thought he'd taken everything—the facilities, the equipment, the brand—all nationalized overnight. What he didn't know was that the Bacardi family had already smuggled out the only thing that actually mattered out of Cuba: the yeast strain. Facundo Bacardi had cultivated a specific yeast in Santiago de Cuba since 1862, filtering rum through charcoal and refining the recipe for nearly 100 years. Without it, the flavor couldn't be replicated. Castro tried—the Cuban government produced their own rum from the seized distillery and couldn't match it. The Bacardi family rebuilt in Puerto Rico, Mexico, and the Bahamas and kept selling. The bat on the label? A colony that had lived in the rafters of the original distillery became the logo. Bacardi is now the largest privately owned spirits company in the world. The original distillery in Santiago de Cuba still exists—the Cuban government still runs it. The bats are still there.
